t: Vinča settlements were larger than those of almost every other European culture of their time; Vinča-Belo Brdo covered 29 hectares with up to 2,500 people.
The Vinča site of Pločnik has produced the earliest copper tools in the world, though copper was used mostly for ornaments while working tools stayed of stone, bone and antler.
Whether the culture grew out of the local Starčevo culture or came with a new movement of people from Anatolia is still undecided.
dyk: The Vinča symbols incised on objects of the culture are conjectured by some to be the earliest form of proto-writing.
ev: The Vinča culture began, according to 600 radiocarbon dates published in 2016
The Divostin site was occupied twice, with an estimated 1,028 houses built
Crkvine-Stubline was founded, perhaps housing up to 4,000 people
In the Vinča D phase the centre of the network shifted from Vinča-Belo Brdo to Vršac
The Vinča network lost its cohesion and fell into decline
Miloje Vasić discovered the type site, Vinča-Belo Brdo

f.homeland: Southeastern Europe, mainly modern Serbia but also parts of southern Hungary, western and central Romania (Oltenia, Transylvania), western Bulgaria, eastern Croatia, eastern Bosnia, northern Montenegro and North Macedonia; key sites Vinča-Belo Brdo near Belgrade, Pločnik, Rudna Glava, Divostin, Crkvine-Stubline, Gomolava, Selevac, Tărtăria and Vršac
f.period: 5400/5300–4500 BCE on 600 radiocarbon dates (2016); phases A–D after the type site, with the “Vinča C shock” or Gradac phase (Vinča B2–C1) and a late Vinča D phase, c. 4850–4500 cal BC
f.known: large tell settlements such as Vinča-Belo Brdo; dark-burnished, Black-topped and Rainbow Ware pottery; zoomorphic and anthropomorphic figurines; the Vinča symbols; the earliest known copper smelting and copper tools at Pločnik; copper mining at Rudna Glava; common wheat, oats and flax brought to temperate Europe
f.sources: Excavation of the type site Vinča-Belo Brdo, discovered by Miloje Vasić in 1908; radiocarbon dating (76 dates in 1996, 155 in 2009, 600 in 2016); the syntheses of John Chapman, Colin Renfrew, Ruth Tringham, V. Gordon Childe and Milutin Garašanin; archaeogenetic studies of 2017 and 2018
